modern: My soul, begin this wintry month with your God. The cold snows and the piercing winds all remind you that he keeps his covenant with day and night, and they help assure you that he will also keep the glorious covenant he has made with you in the person of Christ Jesus. He who is true to his word in the turning of the seasons of this poor, sin-polluted world will not prove unfaithful in his dealings with his own dearly loved Son.

Winter in the soul is by no means a comfortable season, and if it is on you just now, it will be very painful to you. But there is this comfort: *the Lord* makes it. He sends the sharp blasts of hardship to nip the buds of expectation; he scatters the frost like ashes over the once green meadows of our joy; he throws out his ice like crumbs, freezing the streams of our delight. He does it all. He is the great Winter King, who rules in the realms of frost, and so you can’t complain. Losses, crosses, heaviness, sickness, poverty and a thousand other ills are sent by the Lord, and come to us with a wise purpose. Frosts kill harmful insects and put a stop to raging diseases; they break up the clods and sweeten the soil. Oh, that such good results would always follow our winters of affliction!

How we value the fire just now! How pleasant its cheerful glow is! Let’s value our Lord the same way, for he is the constant source of warmth and comfort in every time of trouble. Let’s draw near to him, and in him find joy and peace in believing. Let’s wrap ourselves in the warm clothing of his promises, and go out to the work that suits the season; for it would be a poor thing to be like the sluggard who won’t plow because of the cold, for he will beg in summer and have nothing.

modern:
If we complained less and praised more, we would be happier, and God would be more glorified. Let’s praise God every day for *common mercies*: common, as we often call them, and yet so priceless that when we lose them we are ready to perish. Let’s bless God for the eyes we see the sun with, for the health and strength to walk out of doors, for the bread we eat, for the clothes we wear. Let’s praise him that we aren’t thrown out among the hopeless or locked up among the guilty; let’s thank him for liberty, for friends, for family ties and comforts; let’s praise him, in fact, for everything we receive from his generous hand, for we deserve little and yet are most richly supplied.

But, dear friends, the sweetest and loudest note in our songs of praise should be *redeeming love*. God’s acts of redemption toward his chosen are forever the favorite themes of their praise. If we know what redemption means, let’s not hold back our songs of thanksgiving. We have been redeemed from the power of our corruptions, lifted out of the depth of sin we were plunged in by nature. We have been led to the cross of Christ; our shackles of guilt have been broken off; we are no longer slaves but children of the living God, and we can look ahead to the time when we will be presented before the throne without spot or wrinkle or any such thing. Even now by faith we wave the palm branch, and wrap ourselves in the fine linen that is to be our everlasting clothing; and shall we not give thanks unceasingly to the Lord our Redeemer? Child of God, can you be silent? Wake up, wake up, you heirs of glory, and lead your captivity captive, as you cry with David, “Bless the Lord, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name.” Let the new month begin with new songs.

modern:
The Lord’s admiration of his church is very wonderful, and his description of her beauty glows. She isn’t merely *fair*, but “*all* fair.” He sees her in himself, washed in his sin-atoning blood and clothed in his deserving righteousness, and he considers her full of loveliness and beauty. No wonder, since it is only his own perfect excellence he admires; for the holiness, glory and perfection of his church are his own glorious clothes on the back of his own dearly loved bride. She isn’t simply clean, or well proportioned; she is positively lovely and fair! She has real merit! Her deformities of sin are removed; but more than that, through her Lord she has gained a righteousness of merit by which a real beauty is given to her. Believers are given a positive righteousness when they become “accepted in the beloved” ([[Eph.1.6|Eph. 1:6]]).

Nor is the church just barely lovely; she is lovely *beyond compare*. Her Lord calls her “Thou fairest among women.” She has a real worth and excellence that all the nobility and royalty of the world can’t rival. If Jesus could exchange his chosen bride for all the queens and empresses on earth, or even for the angels in heaven, he wouldn’t, for he puts her first and foremost: “fairest among women.” Like the moon, she far outshines the stars. Nor is this an opinion he is ashamed of, for he invites everyone to hear it. He puts a “behold” in front of it, a special mark of exclamation, inviting and catching attention: “*Behold*, thou art fair, my love; *behold*, thou art fair” ([[Song.4.1|Song of Sol. 4:1]]). He publishes his opinion abroad even now, and one day, from the throne of his glory, he will declare it true before the assembled universe. “Come, ye blessed of my Father” ([[Matt.25.34|Matt. 25:34]]) will be his solemn statement of the loveliness of his chosen.

modern:
Nothing can satisfy the whole person but the Lord’s love and the Lord himself. Saints have tried to anchor in other harbors, but they have been driven out of such deadly refuges. Solomon, the wisest of men, was allowed to make experiments for us all, and to do for us what we mustn’t dare to do for ourselves. Here is his testimony in his own words: “So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me. And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced in all my labour: and this was my portion of all my labour. Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.” “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.” What! All of it vanity? O favored king, is there nothing in all your wealth? Nothing in that wide kingdom stretching from the river to the sea? Nothing in Palmyra’s glorious palaces? Nothing in the house of the forest of Lebanon? In all your music and dancing, your wine and luxury, is there nothing? “Nothing,” he says, “but weariness of spirit.” This was his verdict after he had walked the whole round of pleasure.

To embrace our Lord Jesus, to live in his love and be fully sure of our union with him: this is everything. Dear reader, you don’t need to try other ways of life to see whether they are better than the Christian’s. If you roam the whole world, you’ll see no sight like a sight of the Savior’s face. If you could have all the comforts of life but lost your Savior, you would be wretched; but if you win Christ, then even if you rotted in a dungeon, you would find it a paradise; even if you lived unknown or died of famine, you would still be satisfied with favor and full of the goodness of the Lord.

modern: Having declared his church positively full of beauty, our Lord confirms his praise with a precious negative: “There is no spot in thee.” As if it occurred to the Bridegroom that the faultfinding world would hint that he had only mentioned her lovely features and purposely left out the ones that were deformed or defiled, he sums it all up by declaring her fair all over and through and through, and completely free of stain. A spot may soon be removed, and is the very least thing that can spoil beauty; but even from this little blemish the believer is set free in his Lord’s sight. If he had said there is no hideous scar, no horrible deformity, no deadly ulcer, we might have marveled even then; but when he testifies that she is free from the slightest spot, all these other kinds of defilement are included, and the depth of wonder grows. If he had only promised to remove all spots some day, we would have had eternal reason for joy; but when he speaks of it as already done, who can hold back the most intense feelings of satisfaction and delight? O my soul, here is a rich feast for you; eat your fill, and be satisfied with royal delicacies.

Christ Jesus has no quarrel with his bride. She often wanders from him and grieves his Holy Spirit, but he doesn’t let her faults affect his love. He sometimes scolds, but always in the tenderest way, with the kindest intentions: it is “my love” even then. He doesn’t remember our follies or hold hard thoughts against us; he pardons and loves as much after the offense as before it. It’s good for us that he does, for if Jesus held grudges as we do, how could he have fellowship with us? Many a time a believer will get into a sulk with the Lord over some small turn of providence, but our precious Husband knows our silly hearts too well to take offense at our bad manners.

modern: Our God may well be glorious in the eyes of his people, since he has done such wonders for them, in them and by them. *For them*, the Lord Jesus on Calvary routed every enemy, breaking all the enemy’s weapons to pieces by his finished work of obedience, which satisfied God’s justice. By his triumphant resurrection and ascension he completely overturned the hopes of hell, leading captivity captive, making a public show of our enemies, triumphing over them by his cross. Every arrow of guilt Satan might have shot at us is broken, for who can lay anything to the charge of God’s elect? The sharp swords of hellish malice are useless, and so are the endless battles of the serpent’s offspring, for in the middle of the church the lame take the prey, and the feeblest warriors are crowned.

The saved may well adore their Lord for his conquests *in them*, since the arrows of their natural hatred are snapped and the weapons of their rebellion broken. What victories grace has won in our evil hearts! How glorious Jesus is when the will is conquered and sin dethroned! As for our remaining corruptions, they will suffer an equally sure defeat, and every temptation and doubt and fear will be utterly destroyed. In the Salem of our peaceful hearts, the name of Jesus is great beyond compare: he has won our love, and he will wear it. With the same confidence we may look for victories *by us*. We are more than conquerors through him who loved us. By our faith and zeal and holiness we’ll throw down the powers of darkness in the world; we’ll win sinners to Jesus, we’ll overturn false systems, we’ll convert nations, for God is with us, and no one will stand before us. This evening let the Christian warrior chant the war song and get ready for tomorrow’s fight. Greater is he who is in us than he who is in the world.

modern: This should be a great encouragement to try to do good, since even among the vilest of the vile, the most hardened, the most debauched and drunken, God has a chosen people who must be saved. When you take the Word to them, you do it because God has appointed you to be the messenger of life to their souls, and *they must* receive it, for that is how the decree of predestination runs. They are as much redeemed by blood as the saints before the eternal throne. They are Christ’s property, and yet perhaps they love the pub and hate holiness; but if Jesus Christ bought them, he will have them. God isn’t so unfaithful as to forget the price his Son has paid. He won’t let his Son’s substitution be in any case a useless, dead thing. Tens of thousands of the redeemed aren’t born again yet, but born again they must be; and this is our comfort when we go out to them with the life-giving Word of God.

What’s more, Christ prays for these ungodly people before the throne. “Neither pray I for these alone,” says the great Intercessor, “but for *them also which shall believe* on me through their word.” Poor, ignorant souls, they know nothing about praying for themselves, but Jesus prays for them. Their names are on his breastplate, and before long they must bend their stubborn knees and breathe the sigh of repentance before the throne of grace. “The time of figs is not yet.” The appointed moment hasn’t struck; but when it comes, *they will obey*, for God will have his own. *They must*, for the Spirit can’t be resisted when he comes out in the fullness of his power; *they must* become the willing servants of the living God. “My people shall be willing in the day of my power.” “He shall justify many.” “He shall see of the travail of his soul.” “I will divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong.”

modern:
This groaning is universal among the saints; to a greater or lesser degree we all feel it. It isn’t the groan of grumbling or complaint: it is more the note of desire than of distress. Having received a down payment, we long for the whole of our inheritance. We sigh for our whole human nature, in its threefold being of spirit, soul and body, to be set free from the last trace of the fall. We long to put off decay, weakness and dishonor, and to wrap ourselves in incorruption, in immortality, in glory, in the spiritual body the Lord Jesus will give to his people. We long for our adoption as God’s children to be shown openly. “We groan,” but it is “*within ourselves*.” It isn’t the hypocrite’s groan, by which he would make people believe he is a saint because he is miserable. Our sighs are sacred things, too holy to broadcast. We keep our longings for our Lord alone.

Then the apostle says we are “*waiting*,” which teaches us that we aren’t to be petulant, like Jonah or Elijah when they said, “Let me die”; nor are we to whimper and sigh for the end of life because we are tired of work, nor want to escape our present sufferings before the Lord’s will is done. We are to groan for glory, but we are to wait patiently for it, knowing that what the Lord appoints is best. Waiting implies being ready. We are to stand at the door, expecting the Beloved to open it and take us away to himself. This “groaning” is a test. You can judge a person by what he groans for. Some groan for wealth: they worship Mammon. Some groan constantly under the troubles of life: they are merely impatient. But the one who sighs after God, who is uneasy until he is made like Christ, is the blessed one. May God help us to groan for the coming of the Lord and the resurrection he will bring us.

modern: We know of a place in England, still standing, where a portion of bread is handed out to every passerby who asks for it. Whoever the traveler may be, he has only to knock at the door of St. Cross Hospital, and there is the bread for him. Jesus Christ loves sinners so much that he has built a St. Cross Hospital, so that whenever a sinner is hungry, he has only to knock and have his needs supplied. In fact, he has done better: he has attached a bath to this Hospital of the Cross, and whenever a soul is black and filthy, it has only to go there and be washed. The fountain is always full, always effective. No sinner ever went into it and found that it couldn’t wash away his stains. Sins that were scarlet and crimson have all disappeared, and the sinner has been whiter than snow. As if this weren’t enough, there is a wardrobe attached to this Hospital of the Cross, and a sinner who applies simply as a sinner may be clothed from head to foot; and if he wants to be a soldier, he may have not just clothes for everyday wear but armor to cover him from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. If he asks for a sword, he will be given one, and a shield too. Nothing good for him will be refused him. He will have spending money as long as he lives, and an eternal inheritance of glorious treasure when he enters into the joy of his Lord.

If all these things can be had just by knocking at mercy’s door, O my soul, knock hard this morning, and ask great things of your generous Lord. Don’t leave the throne of grace until all your needs have been spread before the Lord, and until by faith you have a comforting expectation that they will all be supplied. No shyness need hold you back when Jesus invites. No unbelief should stop you when Jesus promises. No coldness of heart should restrain you when such blessings are to be had.

modern:
In the vision described in this chapter, the prophet saw four terrible horns. They were pushing this way and that, throwing down the strongest and the mightiest; and the prophet asked, “What are these?” The answer was, “These are the horns which have scattered Israel.” He saw before him a picture of the powers that had oppressed the church of God. There were four horns, for the church is attacked from every side. The prophet might well have been dismayed; but suddenly *four carpenters* appeared before him. He asked, “What shall these do?” These are the men God has found to break those horns to pieces. *God will always find men for his work*, and he will find them at the right time. The prophet didn’t see the carpenters *first*, when there was nothing to do; he saw the “horns” first, and then the “carpenters.” Moreover, the Lord finds *enough men*. He didn’t find three carpenters, but *four*: there were four horns, and there had to be four workmen. God finds *the right men*: not four men with pens to write, not four architects to draw plans, but four carpenters to do rough work.

Rest assured, you who tremble for the ark of God, that when the “horns” grow troublesome, the “carpenters” will be found. You needn’t fret over the weakness of the church of God at any moment. The brave reformer who will shake the nations may be growing up unknown; Chrysostoms may come out of our Ragged Schools, and Augustines from the thickest darkness of London’s poverty. The Lord knows where to find his servants. He has a multitude of mighty men waiting in ambush, and at his word they will spring up for battle, “for the battle is the Lord’s,” and he will win the victory for himself. Let’s stay faithful to Christ, and at the right time he will raise up a defense for us, whether in the day of our personal need or in a time of danger for his church.

modern:
The head and the members are of one nature, not like that monstrous image Nebuchadnezzar saw in his dream. Its head was of fine gold, but its belly and thighs were of brass, its legs of iron, and its feet part iron and part clay. Christ’s mystical body is no absurd combination of opposites. The members were mortal, and so Jesus died; the glorified Head is immortal, and so the body is immortal too, for this is how the record stands: “Because I live, ye shall live also.” As our loving Head is, so is the body, and every member in particular. A chosen Head and chosen members; an accepted Head and accepted members; a living Head and living members. If the head is pure gold, all the parts of the body are pure gold too. So there is a double union of nature as the basis for the closest fellowship.

Pause here, devout reader, and see whether you can think without ecstatic amazement about the infinite condescension of the Son of God in raising your wretchedness into blessed union with his glory. You are so lowly that, remembering you must die, you may say to corruption, “Thou art my father,” and to the worm, “Thou art my sister”; and yet in Christ you are so honored that you can say to the Almighty, “Abba, Father,” and to the God made flesh, “Thou art my brother and my husband.” Surely, if being related to ancient and noble families makes people think highly of themselves, we have reason to boast above them all. Let the poorest and most despised believer take hold of this privilege. Don’t let senseless laziness make him neglect to trace his family tree, and let him allow no foolish attachment to present vanities to fill his thoughts and crowd out this glorious, heavenly honor of union with Christ.

modern: “One like unto the Son of Man” appeared to John on Patmos, and the beloved disciple noticed that he wore a sash of gold. *A sash*, for Jesus never let his belt hang loose while he was on earth, but always stood ready for service; and now before the eternal throne he doesn’t pause his holy ministry, but as a priest he is wrapped in “the curious girdle of the ephod.” It is good for us that he hasn’t stopped carrying out his offices of love for us, since one of our choicest safeguards is this: he always lives to make intercession for us. Jesus is never idle; his robes are never loosened as though his work were over; he diligently carries on the cause of his people. *A golden sash*, to show the excellence of his service, the royalty of his person, the dignity of his position and the glory of his reward. He no longer cries out from the dust, but pleads with authority, a King as well as a Priest. Our cause is safe enough in the hands of our enthroned Melchizedek.

Our Lord gives all his people an example. We must never unfasten our belts. This isn’t the time for lying back at ease; it is the season of service and warfare. We need to buckle the belt of truth more and more tightly around our waist. It is a golden belt, and so it will be our richest ornament, and we badly need it; for a heart that isn’t well braced with the truth as it is in Jesus, and with the faithfulness the Spirit works in us, will easily be tangled up in the things of this life and tripped by the snares of temptation. It’s no use having the Scriptures unless we bind them around us like a belt, surrounding our whole nature, keeping every part of our character in order and holding our whole self together. If in heaven Jesus doesn’t take off his belt, much less may we on earth. So stand firm, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist.

modern: Walk the streets by moonlight, if you dare, and you’ll see sinners then. Watch when the night is dark, the wind is howling and the lock pick is grating in the door, and you’ll see sinners then. Go to that jail over there and walk through the wards, and look at the men with heavy, overhanging brows, men you wouldn’t want to meet at night, and there are sinners there. Go to the reform schools and notice those who have shown a rampant juvenile depravity, and you’ll see sinners there. Go across the seas to the place where a man will gnaw a bone with human flesh still reeking on it, and there is a sinner there. Go where you like, you needn’t ransack the earth to find sinners, for they are common enough; you can find them in every lane and street of every city and town and village and hamlet. It is for such people that Jesus died. If you pick out for me the coarsest specimen of humanity, if only he is born of woman, I will still have hope for him, because Jesus Christ has come to seek and to save *sinners*. Electing love has chosen some of the worst to be made the best. Grace turns pebbles from the brook into jewels for the royal crown. He transforms worthless slag into pure gold. Redeeming love has set apart many of the worst of humankind to be the reward of the Savior’s suffering. Effectual grace calls many of the vilest of the vile to sit at the table of mercy, so let no one despair.

Reader, by that love looking out of Jesus’ tearful eyes, by that love streaming from those bleeding wounds, by that faithful love, that strong love, that pure, unselfish and lasting love; by the heart and the deepest compassion of the Savior, we solemnly beg you: don’t turn away as though it were nothing to you, but believe on him and you will be saved. Trust your soul to him, and he will bring you to his Father’s right hand in everlasting glory.

modern:
Paul’s great aim was not just to instruct and improve people, but to save them. Anything less would have disappointed him; he wanted people renewed in heart, forgiven, made holy; in fact, saved. Have our Christian labors been aimed at anything lower than this great goal? Then let’s mend our ways, for what good will it do at the last great day to have taught people and improved their morals, if they appear before God unsaved? Our skirts will be blood-red if all through life we have aimed at lesser goals and forgotten that people needed to be saved. Paul knew how ruined human nature is, and didn’t try to educate it, but to save it. He saw people sinking to hell, and didn’t talk of refining them, but of saving them from the wrath to come. To bring about their salvation, he gave himself with untiring zeal to spreading the gospel, to warning people and begging them to be reconciled to God. His prayers were persistent and his labors unceasing. Saving souls was his consuming passion, his ambition, his calling. He became a servant to everyone, toiling for the human race, feeling a woe within him if he didn’t preach the gospel. He set aside his preferences to avoid prejudice; he gave up his own will in matters that didn’t matter; and if people would only receive the gospel, he raised no questions about forms or ceremonies: the gospel was the one all-important business for him. If he might save some, he would be content. This was the crown he strove for, the one and sufficient reward of all his labors and self-denial.

Dear reader, have you and I lived to win souls at this noble rate? Are we possessed by the same all-absorbing desire? If not, why not? Jesus died for sinners; can’t we live for them? Where is our tenderness? Where is our love for Christ, if we don’t seek his honor in the salvation of people? Oh, that the Lord would soak us through and through with an undying zeal for the souls of men.

modern: We can take this to refer to *justification*. “They shall walk in white”: that is, they will enjoy a constant sense of their own justification by faith; they will understand that the righteousness of Christ is credited to them, that they have all been washed and made whiter than newly fallen snow.

Again, it refers to *joy and gladness*, for white robes were festival clothes among the Jews. Those who haven’t defiled their garments will always have bright faces; they’ll understand what Solomon meant when he said, “Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart. Let thy garments be always white, for God hath accepted thy works.” Whoever is accepted by God will wear white garments of joy and gladness as he walks in sweet fellowship with the Lord Jesus. Why so many doubts, so much misery and mourning? It is because so many believers defile their garments with sin and error, and so they lose the joy of their salvation and the comforting fellowship of the Lord Jesus; they don’t walk in white here below.

The promise also refers to *walking in white before the throne of God*. Those who haven’t defiled their garments here will most certainly walk in white up there, where the white-robed hosts sing endless hallelujahs to the Most High. They will have joys beyond imagining, happiness beyond a dream, bliss that imagination doesn’t know, blessedness that even the stretch of desire hasn’t reached. The “undefiled in the way” will have all this, not by merit or by works, but by grace. They will walk with Christ in white, for he has made them “worthy.” In his sweet company they will drink from the living fountains of waters.

modern: All God’s gifts are prepared gifts, stored up ahead for needs he foresaw. He anticipates our needs, and out of the fullness he has stored up in Christ Jesus, he provides from his goodness for the poor. You can trust him for every need that can arise, for he has foreknown every one of them without fail. In every situation he can say of us, “I knew you would be this and that.” A man goes on a journey across the desert, and when he has traveled a day and pitched his tent, he finds he needs many comforts and necessities he didn’t bring in his baggage. “Ah!” he says, “I didn’t foresee this. If I had this journey to make again, I’d bring these things with me; they’re so necessary to my comfort.” But God has noted with a foreseeing eye all the needs of his poor wandering children, and when those needs arise, the supplies are ready. It is goodness he has prepared for the poor in heart, goodness and nothing but goodness. “My grace is sufficient for thee.” “As thy days, so shall thy strength be.”

Reader, is your heart heavy this evening? God knew it would be; the comfort your heart needs is stored in the sweet assurance of this text. You are poor and needy, but he has thought about you, and has in store for you the exact blessing you need. Plead the promise, believe it and receive its fulfillment. Do you feel that you were never so aware of your vileness as you are now? Look, the crimson fountain is still open, with all its old power, to wash your sin away. You will never get into such a position that Christ can’t help you. No pinch will ever come in your spiritual affairs that Jesus Christ won’t be equal to, for your whole story has been foreknown and provided for in Jesus.

modern:
God often *delays in answering prayer*. We have several examples of this in Scripture. Jacob didn’t get the blessing from the angel until close to dawn; he had to wrestle all night for it. The poor Syrophenician woman got no answer at all for a long while. Paul begged the Lord *three times* that “the thorn in the flesh” might be taken from him, and he got no assurance that it would be taken away, but instead a promise that God’s grace would be enough for him. If you have been knocking at the gate of mercy and have had no answer, shall I tell you why the mighty Maker hasn’t opened the door and let you in? Our Father has reasons of his own for keeping us waiting like this. Sometimes it is to show his power and his sovereignty, so that people may know that Jehovah has the right to give or to withhold.

More often the delay is for our good. Perhaps you are kept waiting so that your desires may grow more fervent. God knows that delay will sharpen and increase desire, and that if he keeps you waiting, you’ll see your need more clearly and seek more earnestly, and you’ll value the mercy all the more for its long delay. There may also be something wrong in you that needs to be removed before the joy of the Lord is given. Perhaps your views of the gospel plan are confused, or you may be placing some little reliance on yourself instead of trusting simply and entirely in the Lord Jesus. Or God makes you wait a while so that he can display the riches of his grace to you all the more fully at last. Your prayers are all filed in heaven, and if they aren’t answered immediately, they certainly aren’t forgotten; in a little while they will be fulfilled to your delight and satisfaction. Don’t let despair make you silent, but keep on steadily in earnest prayer.

modern:
Peace and rest don’t belong to the unregenerate; they are the special possession of the Lord’s people, and theirs alone. The God of peace gives perfect peace to those whose hearts are fixed on him. When man had not yet fallen, his God gave him the flowery bowers of Eden as his quiet resting places; but how soon sin blighted that lovely home of innocence! In the day of universal wrath, when the flood swept away a guilty race, the chosen family were kept safe and quiet in the resting place of the ark, which carried them from the old condemned world into the new earth of the rainbow and the covenant, a type of Jesus, the ark of our salvation. Israel rested safely in their blood-sprinkled houses in Egypt when the destroying angel struck down the firstborn; and in the wilderness the shade of the pillar of cloud and the flowing rock gave the weary pilgrims sweet rest.

At this hour we rest in the promises of our faithful God, knowing that his words are full of truth and power; we rest in the teachings of his word, which are comfort itself; we rest in the covenant of his grace, which is a harbor of delight. We are more highly favored than David in the cave of Adullam, or Jonah under his gourd, for no one can invade or destroy our shelter. The person of Jesus is the quiet resting place of his people, and when we draw near to him in the breaking of bread, in hearing the word, in searching the Scriptures, in prayer or praise, we find that every way of coming to him brings peace back to our spirits.

modern: Even the sweetest visits from Christ: how short they are, and how fleeting! One moment our eyes see him, and we rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory; but again a little while and we don’t see him, for our Beloved withdraws from us. Like a gazelle or a young deer he leaps over the mountains of division; he has gone to the land of spices, and no longer feeds among the lilies.

Oh, how sweet is the prospect of the time when we won’t see him at a distance, but face to face; when he won’t be like a traveler staying only for a night, but will hold us forever in the embrace of his glory. We won’t see him for a little while, but

In heaven there will be no interruptions from worry or sin; no weeping will dim our eyes; no earthly business will distract our happy thoughts; nothing will stop us from gazing forever on the Sun of Righteousness with eyes that never tire. Oh, if it is so sweet to see him now and then, how sweet to gaze on that blessed face forever, and never have a cloud roll between, and never have to turn our eyes away to look at a world of weariness and woe! Blessed day, when will you dawn? Rise, O sun that never sets! The joys of the senses may leave us as soon as they like, for this will make glorious amends. If to die is only to enter into uninterrupted fellowship with Jesus, then death is gain indeed, and the bitter drop is swallowed up in a sea of victory.

modern:
There are many points of interest in Lydia’s conversion. It was brought about by *the circumstances of providence*. She was a seller of purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, but just at the right time to hear Paul we find her at Philippi; providence, the handmaid of grace, led her to the right spot. Again, *grace was preparing her soul for the blessing*: grace preparing for grace. She didn’t know the Savior, but as a Jewish woman she knew many truths that were excellent stepping-stones to a knowledge of Jesus. Her conversion took place in the use of the means. On the Sabbath she went where prayer was usually made, and there prayer was heard. Never neglect the means of grace. God *may* bless us when we aren’t in his house, but we have more reason to hope that he *will* when we are in fellowship with his saints.

Notice the words, “Whose heart *the Lord* opened.” She didn’t open her own heart. Her prayers didn’t do it; Paul didn’t do it. The Lord himself must open the heart to receive the things that make for our peace. He alone can put the key into the hole of the door, open it and get in himself. He is the heart’s master, as he is the heart’s maker. The first outward evidence of the opened heart was *obedience*. As soon as Lydia had believed in Jesus, she was baptized. It is a sweet sign of a humble and broken heart when the child of God is willing to obey a command that isn’t essential to his salvation and isn’t forced on him by a selfish fear of condemnation, but is a simple act of obedience and of fellowship with his Master. The next evidence was *love*, showing itself in acts of grateful kindness to the apostles. Love for the saints has always been a mark of the true convert. Those who do nothing for Christ or his church give poor evidence of an “opened” heart. Lord, always give me an opened heart.

modern: Heaven is a place where we will never sin, where we can stop our constant watch against a tireless enemy, because there will be no tempter to trap our feet. There the wicked stop troubling and the weary are at rest. Heaven is the “undefiled inheritance”; it is the land of perfect holiness, and so of complete security. But don’t the saints sometimes taste the joys of blissful security even on earth? The teaching of God’s word is that all who are united to the Lamb are safe; that all the righteous will hold on their way; that those who have committed their souls to Christ’s keeping will find him a faithful and unchanging keeper. Held up by such teaching, we can enjoy security even on earth: not that high and glorious security that frees us from every slip, but the holy security that comes from Jesus’ sure promise that no one who believes in him will ever perish, but will be with him where he is. Believer, let’s often think with joy about the teaching of the perseverance of the saints, and honor the faithfulness of our God by a holy confidence in him.

May our God bring home to you a sense of your safety in Christ Jesus! May he assure you that your name is engraved on his hand, and whisper in your ear the promise, “Fear not, I am with thee.” Look at him, the great Surety of the covenant, as faithful and true, and so bound and committed to present you, the weakest of the family, with all the chosen race, before the throne of God. In such sweet thoughts you will drink the juice of the spiced wine of the Lord’s pomegranate, and taste the dainty fruits of paradise. You will have a foretaste of the joys that thrill the souls of the perfect saints above, if you can believe with unstaggering faith that *“faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it.”*

modern: To what select order of officials was this word spoken? To kings who proudly boast of a divine right? Ah, no! Too often they serve themselves or Satan, and forget the God whose patience lets them wear their mock majesty for their little hour. Is the apostle speaking, then, to the so-called “right reverend fathers in God,” the bishops, or to “the venerable the archdeacons”? No, indeed; Paul knew nothing of these mere human inventions. This word wasn’t spoken even to pastors and teachers, or to the wealthy and respected among believers, but to servants; yes, and to slaves. Among the toiling masses, the hired workers, the day laborers, the domestic servants, the drudges of the kitchen, the apostle found, as we still find, some of the Lord’s chosen, and to them he says, “Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ.” This saying ennobles the weary routine of earthly work and puts a halo around the humblest jobs. Washing feet may be menial, but washing *his* feet is royal work. Untying sandal straps is poor work, but untying the great Master’s sandal is a princely privilege. The shop, the barn, the scullery and the smithy become temples when men and women do everything to the glory of God! Then “divine service” isn’t a matter of a few hours and a few places, but all of life becomes holiness to the Lord, and every place and thing is as holy as the tabernacle and its golden lampstand.

modern: What he has done once, he will do again. Human ways change, but God’s ways are everlasting. There are many reasons for this most comforting truth; among them are these. The Lord’s ways are *the result of wise deliberation*: he orders all things according to the counsel of his own will. Human action is often the hasty result of passion or fear, and is followed by regret and change; but nothing can take the Almighty by surprise, or happen any differently than he has foreseen. His ways *grow out of an unchanging character*, and in them God’s fixed and settled attributes can be clearly seen. Unless the Eternal One himself can change, his ways, which are himself in action, must remain the same forever. Is he eternally just, gracious, faithful, wise and tender? Then his ways must always be marked by the same excellences. Beings act according to their nature; when their nature changes, their conduct changes too. But since God can’t know even the shadow of turning, his ways will remain the same everlastingly. Moreover, there is no outside reason that could reverse God’s ways, since they are *the embodiment of irresistible might*. The prophet says that the earth is split with rivers, the mountains tremble, the deep lifts up its hands, and the sun and moon stand still, when Jehovah marches out for the salvation of his people. Who can hold back his hand, or say to him, What are you doing? But it isn’t might alone that gives stability; God’s ways are *the showing of the eternal principles of right*, and so they can never pass away. Wrong breeds decay and leads to ruin, but the true and the good have a life in them that the ages can’t lessen.
This morning let’s go to our heavenly Father with confidence, remembering that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever, and that in him the Lord is always gracious to his people.

modern:
Believer, here is a sorrowful truth! You are dearly loved by the Lord, redeemed by blood, called by grace, kept safe in Christ Jesus, accepted in the Beloved, on your way to heaven; and yet “thou hast dealt treacherously” with God, your best friend; treacherously with Jesus, whose you are; treacherously with the Holy Spirit, by whom you have been made alive to eternal life! How treacherous you have been in the matter of vows and promises. Do you remember the love of your engagement, that happy time, the springtime of your spiritual life? Oh, how closely you clung to your Master then, saying, “He’ll never accuse me of not caring; my feet will never grow slow in his service; I won’t let my heart wander after other loves; in him is every store of sweetness beyond words. I give it all up for my Lord Jesus’ sake.” Has it been so? Sadly, if conscience speaks, it will say, “He who promised so well has done very badly. Prayer has often been rushed: it has been short, but not sweet; brief, but not fervent. Fellowship with Christ has been forgotten. Instead of a heavenly mind there have been earthly worries, worldly vanities and thoughts of evil. Instead of service there has been disobedience; instead of fervor, lukewarmness; instead of patience, irritability; instead of faith, confidence in an arm of flesh; and as a soldier of the cross there has been cowardice, disobedience and desertion, to a very shameful degree.”

“Thou hast dealt treacherously.” Treachery to Jesus! What words can be used to condemn it? Words do little good: let our repentant thoughts curse the sin that is so surely in us. Treacherous to your wounds, O Jesus! Forgive us, and let us not sin again! How shameful to be treacherous to him who never forgets us, but who stands today with our names engraved on his breastplate before the eternal throne.

modern: Salt was used in every offering made by fire to the Lord, and because it preserves and purifies, it was a welcome picture of God’s grace in the soul. It’s worth noticing that when Artaxerxes gave salt to Ezra the priest, he set no limit on the amount; and we can be quite sure that when the King of kings hands out grace among his royal priesthood, *he* doesn’t cut the supply short. We are often cramped in ourselves, but never in the Lord. Whoever chooses to gather much manna will find he can have as much as he wants. There is no famine in Jerusalem so bad that the citizens must eat their bread by weight and drink their water by measure. Some things in the plan of grace are measured: our vinegar and gall, for instance, are given us so exactly that we never have a single drop too much. But no limit is set on the salt of grace: “Ask what thou wilt and it shall be given unto thee.” Parents need to lock up the fruit cupboard and the jam jars, but there’s no need to keep the salt box under lock and key, for few children will eat too greedily from that. A man may have too much money or too much honor, but he can’t have too much grace. When Jeshurun grew fat in the flesh, he kicked against God; but there’s no fear of anyone becoming too full of grace: an *overdose* of grace is impossible. More wealth brings more worry, but more grace brings more joy. Increased wisdom is increased sorrow, but abundance of the Spirit is fullness of joy. Believer, go to the throne for a large supply of heavenly salt. It will season your afflictions, which are tasteless without salt; it will preserve your heart, which goes bad if salt is missing; and it will kill your sins, as salt kills reptiles. You need much; seek much, and have much.

modern: The church is pictured most instructively as a building put up by heavenly power and designed by divine skill. Such a spiritual house mustn’t be dark, for the Israelites had light in their homes; so there must be windows to let the light in and to let those who live there look out. These windows are *precious*, like agates: the ways the church sees her Lord and heaven and spiritual truth in general are to be valued as highly as can be. Agates are *not the most transparent* of gems; at best they are only half clear:

*Faith* is one of these precious agate windows, but sadly it is often so misty and clouded that we see only dimly and mistake much of what we do see. Yet if we can’t look through windows of diamonds and know even as we are known, it is a glorious thing to see the altogether lovely One, even if the glass is as hazy as agate. *Experience* is another of these dim but precious windows. It gives us a soft, holy light, in which we see the sufferings of the Man of Sorrows through our own afflictions. Our weak eyes couldn’t bear windows of clear glass letting in the Master’s glory; but when they are dimmed with weeping, the beams of the Sun of Righteousness are softened, and shine through the windows of agate with a gentle radiance, soothing beyond words to tempted souls. *Sanctification*, as it makes us like our Lord, is another agate window. Only as we become heavenly can we understand heavenly things. The pure in heart see a pure God. Those who are like Jesus see him as he is. Because we are so little like him, the window is only agate; because we are somewhat like him, it is agate. We thank God for what we have, and long for more. When will we see God and Jesus, and heaven and truth, face to face?

modern: They go from *strength to strength*. There are various translations of these words, but all of them carry the idea of progress.

Our own good Authorized Version is enough for us this morning: “They go from strength to strength.” That is, they grow stronger and stronger. Usually, when we walk, we go from strength to weakness. We start out fresh and in good shape for our journey, but by and by the road is rough and the sun is hot; we sit down by the roadside, and then drag ourselves painfully on our weary way again. But the Christian pilgrim, having received fresh supplies of grace, is as vigorous after years of hard travel and struggle as when he first set out. He may not be quite so elated and buoyant, nor perhaps quite so hot and hasty in his zeal as he once was, but he is much stronger in everything that makes for real power, and he travels, if more slowly, far more surely. Some gray-haired veterans have been as firm in their grip on the truth, and as zealous in spreading it, as they were in their younger days. But sadly, it must be admitted that it is often otherwise, for the love of many grows cold and sin abounds. That is their own sin, though, and not the fault of the promise, which still holds good: “The youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall, but they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles, they shall run and not be weary, and they shall walk and not faint.” Fretful spirits sit down and worry about the future. “Alas!” say they, “we go from affliction to affliction.” Very true, you of little faith; but you also go from strength to strength. You’ll never find a bundle of affliction that doesn’t have enough grace bound up in the middle of it. God will give the strength of a grown man along with the load that is given to grown shoulders.

modern: The Lord Jesus Christ acted, in all he did, as a great public representative, and his dying on the cross was in effect the dying of all his people. In him all his saints paid justice what was due and made atonement to divine vengeance for all their sins. The apostle to the Gentiles loved to think that, as one of Christ’s chosen people, he died on the cross in Christ. He did more than believe this as a doctrine; he accepted it confidently and rested his hope on it. He believed that because of Christ’s death he had satisfied God’s justice and found reconciliation with God. Dear friend, what a blessed thing it is when the soul can, so to speak, stretch itself out on the cross of Christ and feel, “I am dead; the law has killed me, and so I am free from its power, because in my Surety I have borne the curse, and in the person of my Substitute everything the law could do to condemn me has been carried out on me, for I am crucified with Christ.”

But Paul meant even more than this. He didn’t only believe in Christ’s death and trust in it; he actually felt its power in himself, crucifying his old corrupt nature. When he saw the pleasures of sin, he said, “I cannot enjoy these: I am dead to them.” That is the experience of every true Christian. Having received Christ, he is to this world like someone completely dead. Yet while he is aware of being dead to the world, he can at the same time exclaim with the apostle, “Nevertheless I live.” He is fully alive to God. The Christian’s life is a matchless riddle. No worldly person can understand it; even the believer himself can’t understand it. Dead, yet alive! Crucified with Christ, and yet at the same time risen with Christ in newness of life! Union with the suffering, bleeding Savior, and death to the world and to sin, are soul-cheering things. Oh, for more enjoyment of them!

modern:
Both of them loved Naomi, and so they set out with her on her return to the land of Judah. But the hour of testing came. Naomi most unselfishly laid before each of them the trials that awaited them, and told them that if they cared for ease and comfort, they should go back to their friends in Moab. At first both of them declared that they would throw in their lot with the Lord’s people; but on further thought Orpah, with much grief and a respectful kiss, left her mother-in-law and her people and her God, and went back to her idol-worshiping friends, while Ruth gave herself with all her heart to the God of her mother-in-law. It’s one thing to love the ways of the Lord when all is fair, and quite another to hold fast to them through every discouragement and difficulty. The kiss of outward profession is very cheap and easy; but practical holding fast to the Lord, which must show itself in holy decision for truth and holiness, is no small matter.

How do things stand with us? Is our heart fixed on Jesus? Is the sacrifice bound with cords to the horns of the altar? Have we counted the cost, and are we solemnly ready to suffer every worldly loss for the Master’s sake? The gain afterward will be a rich reward, for Egypt’s treasures aren’t to be compared with the glory to be revealed. Orpah is heard of no more; in easy comfort and idol-worshiping pleasure her life fades into the gloom of death. But Ruth lives in history and in heaven, for grace has placed her in the noble line from which came the King of kings. Blessed among women will those be who for Christ’s sake can give up everything; but forgotten, and worse than forgotten, will those be who in the hour of temptation do violence to conscience and turn back to the world. Oh, that this morning we may not be content with the form of devotion, which may be no better than Orpah’s kiss; but may the Holy Spirit work in us a holding fast of our whole heart to our Lord Jesus.

modern: Not only what is seen of the church of God, but what is unseen, is beautiful and precious. Foundations are out of sight, and as long as they are firm, nobody expects them to be valuable; but in Jehovah’s work everything is of a piece: nothing skimped, nothing shabby. The deep foundations of the work of grace are like sapphires in their preciousness; no human mind can measure their glory. We build on the *covenant of grace*, which is firmer than adamant and as lasting as jewels, on which the years spend themselves in vain. Sapphire foundations are eternal, and the covenant lasts as long as the Almighty lives. Another foundation is *the person of the Lord Jesus*, clear and spotless, everlasting and beautiful as the sapphire, blending in one the deep blue of earth’s ever-rolling ocean and the azure of its all-embracing sky. Once our Lord might have been compared to the ruby, as he stood covered with his own blood; but now we see him shining with the soft blue of love: love that overflows, deep and eternal. Our eternal hopes are built on *the justice and the faithfulness of God*, which are as clear and cloudless as the sapphire. We aren’t saved by a compromise, by mercy defeating justice, or by the law suspending its operation. No, we defy the eagle’s eye to find a flaw in the groundwork of our confidence: our foundation is sapphire, and it will stand the fire.

The Lord himself has laid the foundation of his people’s hopes. It is a matter for serious inquiry whether *our* hopes are built on such a base. Good works and ceremonies aren’t a foundation of sapphires but of wood, hay and stubble; and they aren’t laid by God, but by our own conceit. All foundations will be tested before long: woe to the person whose lofty tower comes crashing down because it was built on quicksand. Whoever is built on sapphires can face storm or fire calmly, for he will stand the test.

modern: The cry of the Christian faith is the gentle word “Come.” The Jewish law harshly said, “Go, watch your steps on the path you must walk. Break the commandments, and you will perish; keep them, and you will live.” The law was a system of terror, driving people before it as with a whip; the gospel draws them with cords of love. Jesus is the good Shepherd going ahead of his sheep, telling them to follow him and always leading them on with the sweet word “Come.” The law repels; the gospel attracts. The law shows the distance between God and man; the gospel bridges that awful gulf and brings the sinner across it.

From the first moment of your spiritual life until you are ushered into glory, Christ’s word to you will be, “*Come, come* unto me.” As a mother holds out her finger to her little child and coaxes it to walk by saying, “*Come*,” so does Jesus. He will always be ahead of you, telling you to follow him as a soldier follows his captain. He will always go before you to pave your way and clear your path, and you will hear his encouraging voice calling you after him all through life; and in the solemn hour of death, the sweet words with which he will usher you into the heavenly world will be, “Come, ye blessed of my Father.”

And further, this isn’t only Christ’s cry to you; if you are a believer, it is also your cry to Christ: “Come! come!” You’ll be longing for his second coming; you’ll be saying, “Come quickly, even so come Lord Jesus.” You’ll be panting for nearer and closer fellowship with him. As his voice to you is “Come,” your answer to him will be, “Come, Lord, and stay with me. Come, and occupy the throne of my heart alone; reign there without a rival, and dedicate me entirely to your service.”

modern:
It is painful to remember that to some degree this charge can be laid at the door of *believers*, who too often are, in a measure, *spiritually numb*. We may well mourn that *we* don’t hear God’s voice as we should: “Yea, thou heardest not.” There are gentle movements of the Holy Spirit in the soul that we ignore; there are whispers of God’s command and of heaven’s love that our leaden minds don’t notice at all. Sadly, we have been *carelessly ignorant*: “Yea, thou knewest not.” There are things within us we should have seen: corruptions that have gained ground unnoticed; sweet affections being blighted like flowers in the frost, untended by us; glimpses of God’s face that we might see if we didn’t wall up the windows of our soul. But we “have not known.” As we think of it, we are humbled in the deepest self-abasement.

How we must adore the grace of God as we learn from the context that all this folly and ignorance on our part *was foreknown by God*, and that in spite of that foreknowledge he has still been pleased to deal with us in mercy! Marvel at the sovereign grace that could choose us with all this in view! Wonder at the price that was paid for us when Christ knew what we would be! He who hung on the cross foresaw us as unbelieving, backsliding, cold of heart, indifferent, careless and lax in prayer, and yet he said, “I am the Lord thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour … Since thou wast precious in my sight, thou hast been honourable, and I have loved thee: therefore will I give men for thee, and people for thy life!” Oh, redemption, how wonderfully you shine when we think how black we are! O Holy Spirit, give us from now on the hearing ear and the understanding heart!

modern:
Notice that Christ delights to think about his church and to look at her beauty. As a bird often comes back to its nest, and as a traveler hurries home, so the mind keeps going back to the one it has chosen. We can’t look too often at the face we love; we always want our precious things in sight. It’s the same with our Lord Jesus. From all eternity “His delights were with the sons of men”; his thoughts rolled on to the time when his chosen would be born into the world; he saw them in the mirror of his foreknowledge. “In thy book,” he says, “all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them” ([[Ps.139.16|Ps. 139:16]]). When the world was set on its pillars, he was there, and he set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel. Many times before he took flesh, he came down to this lower earth in the likeness of a man: on the plains of Mamre ([[Gen.18|Gen. 18]]), by the brook Jabbok ([[Gen.32.24|Gen. 32:24]]-[[Gen.32.30|30]]), beneath the walls of Jericho ([[Josh.5.13|Jos. 5:13]]), and in the fiery furnace of Babylon ([[Dan.3.19|Dan. 3:19]], [[Dan.3.25|25]]), the Son of Man visited his people. Because his soul delighted in them, he couldn’t rest away from them, for his heart longed for them.

They were never absent from his heart, for he had written their names on his hands and engraved them on his side. As the breastplate with the names of the tribes of Israel was the most brilliant ornament the high priest wore, so the names of Christ’s chosen were his most precious jewels, glittering on his heart. We may often forget to meditate on the perfections of our Lord, but he never stops remembering us. Let’s scold ourselves for our past forgetfulness, and pray for grace always to keep him in fondest remembrance. Lord, paint the image of your Son on the eyeballs of my soul.

modern: Jesus, the great I AM, is the entrance into the true church and the way of access to God himself. He gives the person who comes to God through him four choice privileges.

1. *He shall be saved*. The fleeing manslayer passed through the gate of the city of refuge and was safe. Noah entered the door of the ark and was secure. No one can be lost who takes Jesus as the door of faith for his soul. Entering peace through Jesus guarantees entering heaven by the same door. Jesus is the only door, an open door, a wide door, a safe door; and blessed is the one who rests all his hope of getting into glory on the crucified Redeemer.

2. *He shall go in*. He will have the privilege of going in among the family of God, sharing the children’s bread and taking part in all their honors and enjoyments. He will go into the rooms of fellowship, to the banquets of love, to the treasures of the covenant, to the storehouses of the promises. He will go in to the King of kings in the power of the Holy Spirit, and the secret of the Lord will be with him.

3. *He shall go out*. This blessing is often forgotten. We go out into the world to work and suffer, but what a mercy to go in the name and power of Jesus! We are called to bear witness to the truth, to cheer the downhearted, to warn the careless, to win souls and to glorify God; and as the angel said to Gideon, “Go in this thy might,” so the Lord wants us to go out as his messengers in his name and strength.

4. *He shall find pasture*. Whoever knows Jesus will never go without. Going in and going out will both help him: in fellowship with God he will grow, and in watering others he will be watered himself. Having made Jesus his all, he will find everything in Jesus. His soul will be like a watered garden, like a spring of water whose waters never fail.

modern: *Tearing your clothes* and other outward signs of religious emotion are easily put on and are *often hypocritical*; but feeling true repentance is far harder, and so far less common. People will attend to the most numerous and detailed ceremonial rules, for such things are *pleasing to the flesh*; but true religion is too humbling, too heart-searching, too thorough for the taste of fleshly people. They prefer something showier, flimsier and more worldly. Outward observances are *comforting for a while*: the eye and ear are pleased, self-conceit is fed and self-righteousness is puffed up; but in the end *they deceive*, for at the moment of death and on the day of judgment the soul needs something more solid than ceremonies and rituals to lean on. Without living godliness all religion is utterly empty; offered without a sincere heart, every form of worship is a solemn sham and a shameless mockery of the majesty of heaven.

*Tearing the heart* is *worked by God and solemnly felt*. It is a secret grief that is *experienced personally*, not as a mere form but as a deep, soul-moving work of the Holy Spirit on the inmost heart of each believer. It isn’t something just to be talked about and believed in, but felt keenly and sensitively in every living child of the living God. It is *powerfully humbling* and completely sin-purging; but it is also *a sweet preparation* for the gracious comforts that proud, unhumbled spirits can’t receive. And it *clearly marks out* those who have it, for it belongs to God’s chosen, and to them alone.

The text commands us to tear our hearts, but by nature they are as hard as marble: how can it be done? We must take them to Calvary. A dying Savior’s voice tore the rocks once, and it is just as powerful now. O blessed Spirit, let us hear the death cries of Jesus, and our hearts will be torn, just as people tear their clothes in the day of mourning.

modern:
Every wise merchant will hold a stocktaking now and then, when he will add up his accounts, examine what he has on hand and find out for certain whether his trade is thriving or declining. Everyone who is wise in the kingdom of heaven will cry, “Search me, O God, and try me”; and he will often set apart special times for self-examination, to find out whether things are right between God and his soul. The God we worship is a great searcher of hearts, and long ago his servants knew him as “the Lord which searcheth the heart and trieth the reins of the children of men.” Let me stir you up in his name to make a careful search and a solemn test of your condition, so that you don’t fall short of the promised rest. What every wise person does, and what God himself does with us all, I urge you to do with yourself this evening. Let the oldest saint look well to the foundations of his faith, for gray heads may cover black hearts; and let the young believer not despise the word of warning, for the greenness of youth may be joined to the rottenness of hypocrisy. Every now and then a cedar falls among us. The enemy still keeps sowing weeds among the wheat.

It isn’t my aim to bring doubts and fears into your mind. No, truly; I hope rather that the rough wind of self-examination may help to drive them away. It isn’t security but carnal security we want to kill; not confidence but fleshly confidence we want to overthrow; not peace but false peace we want to destroy. By the precious blood of Christ, which wasn’t shed to make you a hypocrite but so that sincere souls might show forth his praise, I beg you: search and look, so that at the last it won’t be said of you, “Mene, Mene, Tekel: thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.”

modern: If the outcome of the lot belongs to the Lord, whose is the ordering of our whole life? If the simple casting of a lot is guided by him, how much more the events of our whole life, especially when our blessed Savior tells us, “The very hairs of your head are all numbered: not a sparrow falleth to the ground without your Father.” It would bring a holy calm over your mind, dear friend, if you always remembered this. It would free your mind from anxiety so much that you would be better able to walk in patience, quiet and cheerfulness, as a Christian should. When a man is anxious, he can’t pray in faith; when he is troubled about the world, he can’t serve his Master; his thoughts are serving himself. If you would “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness,” all things would then be added to you. You are meddling with Christ’s business and neglecting your own when you fret about your lot and circumstances. You have been trying to do the “providing” and forgetting that your part is to obey. Be wise: see to the obeying, and let Christ manage the providing. Come and look over your Father’s storehouse, and ask whether he will let you starve while he has stored up such abundance in his barn! Look at his merciful heart: see if that can ever prove unkind! Look at his unsearchable wisdom: see if that will ever be at fault. Above all, look up to Jesus Christ your Intercessor, and ask yourself: while he pleads, can your Father deal ungraciously with you? If he remembers even sparrows, will he forget one of the least of his poor children? “Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and he will sustain thee. He will never suffer the righteous to be moved.”

modern:
We could hardly rejoice at the thought of losing the glorious old ocean. The new heavens and the new earth are none the lovelier to our imagination if there is literally to be no great wide sea, with its gleaming waves and shell-strewn shores. Isn’t the text to be read as a metaphor, colored by the dislike with which the Eastern mind always regarded the sea in ancient times? A real physical world without a sea is a mournful thing to imagine: it would be an iron ring without the sapphire that made it precious. There must be a spiritual meaning here. In the new order there will be no *division*. The sea separates nations and cuts peoples off from each other. To John on Patmos the deep waters were like prison walls, shutting him out from his brothers and his work; there will be no such barriers in the world to come. Leagues of rolling waves lie between us and many a relative whom we remember in prayer tonight, but in the bright world we are going to there will be unbroken fellowship for the whole redeemed family. In this sense there will be no more sea.

The sea is the picture of change. With its ebbs and flows, its glassy smoothness and its mountainous waves, its gentle murmurs and its thundering roars, it is never the same for long. Slave of the fickle winds and the changing moon, it is a byword for instability. In this mortal life we have too much of that; earth is constant only in her inconstancy. But in heaven all mournful change will be unknown, and with it all fear of *storm* to wreck our hopes and drown our joys. The sea of glass glows with a glory unbroken by a wave. No storm howls along the peaceful shores of paradise. Soon we will reach that happy land where partings and changes and storms will be over! Jesus will carry us there. Are we in him or not? That is the great question.

modern:
Sometimes the Lord Jesus tells his church his thoughts of love. “He does not think it enough behind her back to tell it, but in her very presence he says, ‘Thou art all fair, my love.’ It is true, this is not his ordinary method; he is a wise lover, and knows when to keep back the intimation of love and when to let it out; but there are times when he will make no secret of it; times when he will put it beyond all dispute in the souls of his people” (R. Erskine’s Sermons). The Holy Spirit is often pleased, in a most gracious way, to bear witness with our spirits to the love of Jesus. He takes the things of Christ and shows them to us. No voice is heard from the clouds and no vision is seen in the night, but we have a testimony surer than either. If an angel flew down from heaven and told the saint in person of the Savior’s love for him, the evidence wouldn’t be one bit more satisfying than what the Holy Spirit bears in the heart.

Ask those of the Lord’s people who have lived nearest to the gates of heaven, and they will tell you they have had seasons when the love of Christ for them was a fact so clear and sure that they could no more doubt it than they could question their own existence. Yes, dear believer, you and I have had times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord, and then our faith has climbed to the topmost heights of assurance. We have had confidence to lean our heads on our Lord’s breast, and we have no more questioned our Master’s love for us than John did in that blessed position; no, not even as much, for the dark question, “Lord, is it I that shall betray thee?” has been put far from us. He has kissed us with the kisses of his mouth, and killed our doubts by the closeness of his embrace. His love has been sweeter than wine to our souls.

modern:
God is a good paymaster. He pays his servants while they are working as well as when they have finished, and one of his payments is this: *an easy conscience*. If you have spoken faithfully about Jesus to one person, when you go to bed at night you are happy to think, “Today I have cleared my conscience of that man’s blood.” There is great *comfort in doing something for Jesus*. Oh, what happiness to place jewels in his crown, and let him see the travail of his soul! There is also a very great reward in *watching the first buds of conviction in a soul*! To say of that girl in the class, “She is tender of heart, I do hope that there is the Lord’s work within.” To go home and pray over that boy who said something in the afternoon that made you think he must know more of God’s truth than you had feared! Oh, the joy of hope! But as for *the joy of success*, it is beyond words. This joy, overwhelming as it is, is a hungry thing: you long for more of it. Being a soul-winner is the happiest thing in the world. With every soul you bring to Christ, you get a new heaven on earth.

But who can imagine the bliss that awaits us above! Oh, how sweet is that sentence, “Enter thou into *the joy of thy Lord*!” Do you know what the joy of Christ is over a saved sinner? This is the very joy we are to have in heaven. Yes, when he mounts the throne, you will mount with him. When the heavens ring with “Well done, well done,” you will share in the reward. You have toiled with him, you have suffered with him, and now you will reign with him; you have sown with him, and you will reap with him. Your face was covered with sweat like his, and your soul grieved over the sins of men as his soul did; now your face will be bright with heaven’s splendor like his, and now your soul will be filled with heavenly joys, just as his is.

modern: This covenant is *divine in its origin*. “*He* hath made with me an everlasting covenant.” Oh, that great word *He*! Stop, my soul. God, the everlasting Father, has actually made a covenant with you; yes, that God who spoke the world into existence by a word, stooping from his majesty, takes hold of your hand and makes a covenant with you. Isn’t it an act whose staggering condescension might thrill our hearts forever, if we could really understand it? “*He* hath made with me a covenant.” A king hasn’t made a covenant with me; that would be something. But the Prince of the kings of the earth, Shaddai, the all-sufficient Lord, the Jehovah of the ages, the everlasting Elohim: “He hath made with me an everlasting covenant.” But notice, it is *particular in its application*. “Yet hath he made with *me* an everlasting covenant.” Here lies its sweetness for each believer. It is nothing to me that he made peace for the world; I want to know whether he made peace for *me*! It is little to me that he has made a covenant; I want to know whether he has made a covenant *with me*. Blessed is the assurance that he has made a covenant with me! If God the Holy Spirit gives me assurance of this, then his salvation is mine, his heart is mine, he himself is mine: *he is my God*.

This covenant is *everlasting in its duration*. An everlasting covenant means a covenant that had no beginning and will never, never end. How sweet, amid all the uncertainties of life, to know that “the foundation of the Lord standeth sure,” and to have God’s own promise, “My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips.” Like dying David, I will sing of this, even though my house isn’t with God as my heart desires.

modern: See with what matchless generosity the Lord provides clothing for his people. They are dressed so that God’s skill is seen producing an unrivaled *embroidered work*, in which every attribute plays its part and every divine beauty is revealed. There is no art like the art shown in our salvation, no skilled workmanship like that seen in the righteousness of the saints. Justification has filled learned pens in every age of the church, and will be the theme of wonder in eternity. God has indeed “curiously wrought it.” With all this elaborate work there is usefulness and durability, like being *shod with badgers’ skins*. The animal meant here is unknown, but its skin covered the tabernacle, and made one of the finest and strongest leathers known. The righteousness that comes from God by faith lasts forever, and whoever is shod with this divine preparation will walk the desert safely, and may even set his foot on the lion and the adder. The purity and dignity of our holy clothing are brought out in *the fine linen*. When the Lord sanctifies his people, they are dressed like priests in pure white; not even the snow outshines them; in the eyes of men and angels they are lovely to look at, and even in the Lord’s eyes they are without spot. Meanwhile the royal clothing is as delicate and rich as *silk*. No expense is spared, no beauty withheld, no delicacy denied.
What then? Is there nothing to draw from this? Surely there is gratitude to be felt and joy to be expressed. Come, my heart, don’t refuse your evening hallelujah! Tune your pipes! Touch your strings!

modern: God has a strong reserve with which to keep this commitment, for he is able to do all things. Believer, until you can drain the ocean of omnipotence dry, until you can break the towering mountains of almighty strength to pieces, you never need to be afraid. Don’t think that human strength will ever be able to overcome the power of God. While the earth’s huge pillars stand, you have reason enough to stay firm in your faith. The same God who steers the earth in its orbit, who feeds the burning furnace of the sun and trims the lamps of heaven, has promised to supply you with strength every day. While he is able to hold up the universe, don’t dream that he will prove unable to keep his own promises. Remember what he did in the days of old, in former generations. Remember how he spoke and it was done; how he commanded and it stood firm. Will he who created the world grow weary? He hangs the world on nothing; will he who does this be unable to support his children? Will he be unfaithful to his word for lack of power? Who is it that holds back the storm? Doesn’t he ride on the wings of the wind, and make the clouds his chariots, and hold the ocean in the hollow of his hand? How can he fail you? When he has put such a faithful promise as this on record, will you for a moment entertain the thought that he has promised more than he can do, and gone beyond his power to fulfill? Ah, no! You can’t doubt any longer.

O you who are my God and my strength, I can believe that this promise will be fulfilled, for the boundless reservoir of your grace can never be exhausted, and the overflowing storehouse of your strength can never be emptied by your friends or robbed by your enemies.

modern:
What is the secret spot that unmistakably marks a child of God? It would be empty presumption to decide this by our own judgment; but God’s word reveals it to us, and we can walk surely where we have revelation to guide us. Now, we are told of our Lord, “to as many as *received him*, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to as many as believed on his name.” Then, if I have received Christ Jesus into my heart, I am a child of God. That receiving is described in the same verse as *believing on the name of Jesus Christ*. If, then, I believe on the name of Jesus Christ, that is, simply trust myself from my heart to the crucified and now exalted Redeemer, I am a member of the family of the Most High. Whatever else I may not have, if I have this, I have the privilege of becoming a child of God. Our Lord Jesus puts it another way: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” Here is the matter in a nutshell. Christ appears as a shepherd to his own sheep, not to others. As soon as he appears, his own sheep recognize him: they trust him and are ready to follow him. He knows them and they know him; there is a knowledge on both sides and a constant connection between them. So the one mark, the sure mark, the unfailing mark of new birth and adoption is a heartfelt faith in the appointed Redeemer.

Reader, are you in doubt? Are you unsure whether you bear the secret mark of God’s children? Then don’t let an hour pass over your head until you have said, “Search me, O God, and know my heart.” Don’t trifle here, I solemnly urge you! If you must trifle anywhere, let it be about some secondary matter: your health, if you like, or the title deeds of your estate; but about your soul, your never-dying soul and its eternal destiny, I beg you to be in earnest. Make sure work for eternity.
